results.summary: This design uses AND gates to drive segments of a number display, with inputs mapped to outputs in a fixed pattern. It is tested by using a multimeter on the beep setting to check for connections between pins. The project requires an external number segment display as hardware. The documentation is minimal and the description is vague, so the exact logic function is not fully clear.

This is a Tiny Tapeout template project that appears to implement some logic involving inputs a through f and outputs including an AND result and pass-through signals. The documentation states that the author does not know how it works or how to test it. No external hardware is listed. The project is essentially undocumented beyond pin names, making its function unclear.

This project has a title and pin names but the documentation describes its operation as 'Magic' and testing as 'Dark magic'. No external hardware is listed. There is no meaningful description of what the design does or how it is used. The documentation is insufficient to determine the design's purpose or behavior.

This design implements AND logic gates whose outputs drive LEDs, with additional pass-through connections intended to light segments of a number eight display. It is tested by switching on pins 1 and 3 to activate the AND gate. The project requires external LEDs as hardware. The documentation is basic and appears to be from an educational exercise.

This project displays numbers on a seven-segment LED display by turning on the correct switches, with a shortcut to display the number one using the first two switches. The pin names are whimsical and do not describe their function. It requires an external LED display. The documentation is thin and the mapping between switches and segments is not clearly explained.

This design always displays the number 7 on a seven-segment LED display regardless of which input switch is turned on, as long as at least one switch is active. It is tested by pressing start and turning on any switch. The project requires an external LED display. The documentation is minimal and the design appears to be a simple fixed-output exercise.

This is a T flip-flop that toggles its output state when the T input is high and a clock pulse is received, providing both Q and inverted Q outputs. It is tested by applying the truth table combinations and observing the outputs. An external LED is suggested for testing. The documentation is clear and includes a truth table, making it a straightforward sequential logic example.

This design is described as implementing a T flip-flop using AND gates and XOR gates, but the pin names mention AND and NOR functions. It provides a direct LED connection for power checking, with outputs on pins 0 and 1. External hardware such as buttons, LEDs, and resistors is listed. The documentation is disorganized and the exact circuit topology is unclear.

This design inverts each input signal, acting as a set of inverters, and is intended as a template for testing and building more complex digital logic circuits. It is tested by toggling input switches and observing the outputs, with suggestions to replace inverters with other logic functions. No external hardware is used. The documentation is contradictory, mentioning OR gates and a clock divider in the title but describing inverters in the text.

This project connects switches to a seven-segment display that is described as an analog clock, with each switch controlling a specific segment. It is tested by toggling the numbered switches and observing which parts of the clock light up. External hardware includes a seven-segment LED display, a set of eight switches, and two tactile push buttons. The documentation is minimal and the description of the clock behavior is vague.
